lead: Real gases do not obey PV = RT, especially near the critical point and at high pressure. The compressibility factor Z = PV/RT measures the departure: Z = 1 means ideal, and Z away from 1 means real. Instead of a separate table for every gas, generalized correlations use reduced temperature and pressure, and sometimes the acentric factor, to read Z from one chart. Chemical engineers use this for quick volume estimates, compressor work, pipeline sizing, and checking cubic equations of state. It is a first estimate, not a substitute for a good equation of state.
prereq: You need: Chapter 2.3 for equations of state and critical constants, and Chapter 2.2 for the ideal gas law.

blocks.text: For one mole, an ideal gas obeys PV = RT. Define the compressibility factor Z = PV/RT. Here P is pressure, V is molar volume, R is the gas constant, and T is absolute temperature. Z is dimensionless. An ideal gas has Z = 1 at every T and P. A real gas has Z below or above 1.

Z below 1 means attractive forces dominate, so the volume is smaller than ideal. Z above 1 means molecular size and repulsion dominate, so the volume is larger than ideal. At very low pressure every gas approaches Z = 1. Near the critical point Z can be far from 1. Z is a function of T and P for each gas, not a constant.

blocks.where: V is molar volume, Z is the compressibility factor, R is the gas constant, T is absolute temperature, and P is pressure.

items: Reduced temperature: T<sub>r</sub> = T/T<sub>c</sub>, where T<sub>c</sub> is the critical temperature.
Reduced pressure: P<sub>r</sub> = P/P<sub>c</sub>, where P<sub>c</sub> is the critical pressure.
Reduced volume: V<sub>r</sub> = V/V<sub>c</sub>, where V<sub>c</sub> is the critical molar volume.
T<sub>r</sub>, P<sub>r</sub> and V<sub>r</sub> are dimensionless.

sections.h3: Corresponding states and the acentric factor

blocks.text: The principle of corresponding states says that fluids at the same T<sub>r</sub> and P<sub>r</sub> have approximately the same Z. This is why one generalized compressibility chart can serve many gases. It is a two-parameter correlation: T<sub>c</sub> and P<sub>c</sub> fix the reduced coordinates.

Simple spherical molecules follow this rule well. Polar molecules and long molecules need a third parameter. The Pitzer acentric factor ω measures the vapour-pressure curve shape and is tabulated with T<sub>c</sub> and P<sub>c</sub>. The three-parameter correlation is Z = Z⁰ + ωZ¹. Read Z⁰ and Z¹ from tables or charts at the given T<sub>r</sub> and P<sub>r</sub>.

blocks.where: Z⁰ is the simple-fluid compressibility factor, Z¹ is its correction, and ω is the Pitzer acentric factor; both Z⁰ and Z¹ depend on T<sub>r</sub> and P<sub>r</sub>.

blocks.text: Some syllabi call this the generalized compressibility factor correlation. For nonpolar gases it is accurate enough for quick design checks. For strongly polar or associating gases, use an equation of state with better mixing rules.

sections.h3: Reading a chart and using generalized equations

items: Look up T<sub>c</sub> and P<sub>c</sub> for the gas.
Compute T<sub>r</sub> = T/T<sub>c</sub> and P<sub>r</sub> = P/P<sub>c</sub>.
Find the curve for T<sub>r</sub> and move to the value P<sub>r</sub> on the horizontal axis.
Read Z from the vertical axis.
Compute V = ZRT/P, keeping R consistent with the pressure and volume units.

blocks.text: A generalized equation of state is an equation written in T<sub>r</sub>, P<sub>r</sub> and ω so that it returns Z directly. A common Pitzer-type form is Z = 1 + (B⁰ + ωB¹)P<sub>r</sub>/T<sub>r</sub>, where B⁰ and B¹ are tabulated functions of T<sub>r</sub>. Charts are graphical versions of such correlations.
T<sub>pc</sub> = Σ y<sub>i</sub>T<sub>c,i</sub>,  P<sub>pc</sub> = Σ y<sub>i</sub>P<sub>c,i</sub>
blocks.where: For a gas mixture, y<sub>i</sub> is the mole fraction and T<sub>c,i</sub>, P<sub>c,i</sub> are component critical constants; use T<sub>pc</sub> and P<sub>pc</sub> as pseudo critical values on the same chart.

figure.caption: The chart path from given T and P to Z and V: at T<sub>r</sub> = 1.2 and P<sub>r</sub> = 2.0 read Z = 0.65, then V = 0.195 L/mol.

spec.title: Reading a generalized chart
spec.aria: Flowchart: given T and P, look up Tc and Pc, compute Tr and Pr, read Z from a generalized chart, then calculate molar volume.

examples.question: A gas has T<sub>c</sub> = 300 K and P<sub>c</sub> = 50 bar. At T = 360 K and P = 100 bar, a generalized chart gives Z = 0.65. Find T<sub>r</sub>, P<sub>r</sub> and the molar volume using R = 0.08314 L bar mol⁻¹ K⁻¹.
examples.check:
R = 0.08314
T = 360.0
P = 100.0
Tc = 300.0
Pc = 50.0
Z = 0.65
Tr = T / Tc
Pr = P / Pc
V = Z * R * T / P
print(round(Tr, 3))
print(round(Pr, 3))
print(round(V, 3))

traps: Using T and P directly on the chart without first computing T<sub>r</sub> and P<sub>r</sub>.
Assuming Z = 1 at high pressure because the gas is called permanent; high pressure usually increases deviation from ideal behaviour.
Mixing units: T must be absolute, P and P<sub>c</sub> must use the same unit, and R must match the chosen pressure and volume units.
Treating a chart reading as exact; generalized charts are approximate, so do not report more digits than the chart supports.
Using the two-parameter chart for a polar gas when the acentric factor or a better equation of state is needed.

quiz.q: Define the compressibility factor Z and state its value for an ideal gas.
quiz.a: Z = PV/RT, where P is pressure, V is molar volume, R is the gas constant, and T is absolute temperature. For an ideal gas Z = 1.

quiz.q: Why do reduced temperature and reduced pressure let one chart serve many gases?
quiz.a: The principle of corresponding states says that fluids at the same T<sub>r</sub> and P<sub>r</sub> have approximately the same Z. Critical constants scale out the differences between gases.

quiz.q: A gas has T<sub>c</sub> = 200 K and P<sub>c</sub> = 40 bar. At T = 400 K and P = 20 bar, a chart gives Z = 0.90. Find T<sub>r</sub>, P<sub>r</sub> and V using R = 0.08314 L bar mol⁻¹ K⁻¹.
Two gases have the same T<sub>r</sub> and P<sub>r</sub> but different Z. What third parameter improves the correlation, and why can it still fail for polar gases?
quiz.a: The Pitzer acentric factor ω improves the correlation through Z = Z⁰ + ωZ¹. Polar and associating gases can still deviate because the correlation does not fully represent hydrogen bonding and strong polarity.

quiz.q: Write the Pitzer three-parameter compressibility correlation.
quiz.a: Z = Z⁰ + ωZ¹, where Z⁰ and Z¹ depend on T<sub>r</sub> and P<sub>r</sub>, and ω is the acentric factor.

quiz.q: What does Z < 1 mean physically for a real gas?
quiz.a: The gas volume is smaller than the ideal-gas volume at the same T and P. Attractive forces dominate over size and repulsion effects.

quiz.q: For T<sub>c</sub> = 300 K, P<sub>c</sub> = 50 bar, T = 360 K and P = 100 bar, Z = 0.65. Find the ideal-gas volume and the percent by which it exceeds the real volume, relative to the real volume.

beyond: Not for the exam. Process simulators use generalized correlations for quick checks and cubic equations of state for final design. The acentric factor appears in Pitzer correlations and in mixing rules for reservoir fluids. Search for Pitzer correlation, Lee-Kesler tables, and corresponding states for mixtures.
